clue.text: One who has to clean up tart?

definitions.text: One who has to clean up

blocks.clueFragment: One who has to clean up
blocks.note: first meaning: someone who scrubs floors and pans
second meaning: British slang for a promiscuous woman

explanation.surface: A pastry chef left to wash up after the tart is baked.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, it sounds like cleaning a pie dish; 'tart' is really the British slang insult, which SCRUBBER also means.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrubber is literally one who scrubs, and in British slang a derogatory word for a loose woman.

clue.text: A supporter of bums on the slippery slope

definitions.text: A supporter of bums on the slippery slope

blocks.clueFragment: A supporter of bums on the slippery slope
blocks.note: surface reading: someone who backs layabouts heading for moral ruin

blocks.clueFragment: A supporter of bums on the slippery slope
blocks.note: setter's reading: a seat carrying skiers' backsides up a snowy mountain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bums' means backsides, not vagrants, and the slippery slope is a literal ski run.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski lift of seats hung from a cable carries seated skiers up the piste.

clue.text: As practised by golfer, Lofty, to be promiscuous?

blocks.note: lofty means high, raised up
to swing is to swap sexual partners

explanation.surface: A golfer nicknamed Lofty is accused of sleeping around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lofty' looks like a nickname for the golfer; it is just the word for high.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer raises the club on the backswing, the upward stroke before hitting the ball.

clue.text: (see 9dn.)
( +26dn.) Rabbit sailor stuck up arse

indicators.note: in a down clue, stuck up means set upwards, so the pair is read from the bottom

blocks.note: to rabbit is British slang for chatter, as is to gab
a tar is an old word for a seaman

explanation.surface: A crude tale of a seaman with a rabbit stuck where it should not be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' wants to be the animal; it is the verb meaning to talk on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: Arse is British slang for an obnoxious fool, and a ratbag is a nasty or contemptible person.

clue.text: Not a clanger to abandon Latin prize instigator

indicators.note: abandoning something means leaving it behind, so that letter is dropped from the build

blocks.note: a flat negative
a bell is a thing that clangs
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin; this is the letter thrown out

explanation.surface: Someone who never drops a clanger walks away from a Latin prize.
explanation.walkthrough: NO BELL loses one L to leave NOBEL; 'clanger' looks like the British word for a blunder but is just a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel founded the Nobel Prizes through his will, so he set the awards going.

clue.text: Bland Gingrich overheard at bar: "Ego's gone"

indicators.note: overheard means caught by ear, so the spoken form of the politician's name is what counts
whatever has gone is no longer there, so that letter is taken away

blocks.note: Newt Gingrich, the US Republican politician, spelt to suit the sound
a rail is a bar
I is the self, the ego; this letter goes from the bar

explanation.surface: The dull Republican is heard in a pub boasting that his ego has vanished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' suggests a pub; it is a rod, and its I is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Neutral describes something without strong flavour or colour, unremarkable and mild.

clue.text: Place iodine in Elton John's rear

indicators.note: the rear of a word is its tail end, so only its closing letter is wanted
the chemical symbol is put in among the other letters

blocks.note: Ben Elton is a British comedian and writer
I is the chemical symbol for iodine
the final letter of John

explanation.surface: A cheeky jab at putting something into the singer's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Elton John reads as one singer; split, Elton is the surname of comedian Ben Elton, and John supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Benin is a West African country, and a country is a place.

clue.text: Incontinence pads should stop this ale-swilling ruler

indicators.note: swilling sloshes liquid around, so the letters of the drink are churned

blocks.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder
a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: A beer-guzzling monarch needs absorbent pads.
explanation.definitionFit: Incontinence pads absorb urine, preventing it escaping, which is what leaking describes.

clue.text: ( & 4dn.) Strong reprimand a sinisterly equipped Hitler could have done with?

definitions.text: a sinisterly equipped Hitler could have done with?

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for a severe telling-off

blocks.clueFragment: a sinisterly equipped Hitler could have done with?
blocks.note: second meaning, read as a pun: supplying a missing testicle on the other side

explanation.walkthrough: The wartime song claimed Hitler had only one ball; sinister means left, so a right one is what he lacked.
explanation.definitionFit: Bollocking is British slang for a fierce scolding, and right is an intensifier, as in a right mess.

clue.text: Makes a bigger bore of many papers

blocks.note: first meaning: widens a drilled hole with a reamer
second meaning: large quantities of paper, a ream being 500 sheets

explanation.surface: A dull person becomes even duller by writing piles of documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' pretends to be a tedious person; it is the width of a hole.
explanation.definitionFit: To ream is to enlarge a hole, and reams are bundles of sheets, hence a great amount of writing.

clue.text: State of endless stink at heart of Italian corruption

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter of the word is lopped off
corruption spoils and distorts, so the letters of the word before it are rearranged
sitting at the heart of something means being placed in its middle

blocks.note: a hum is a bad smell in British slang; it loses its last letter
the word taken letter by letter as the anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A country whose politics reek like the bribery scandals of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian corruption' reads as Italy's 1990s bribery scandals, but corruption is the anagram signal and Italian its fodder; a hum is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: Lithuania is a sovereign Baltic country, and a nation can be called a state.

clue.text: Newspaper-backed Ron is awfully camp

indicators.note: backed here means turned back to front, so the paper's word runs right to left
done awfully means done badly, so those letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
the two words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A tabloid-supported man named Ron is terribly flamboyant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Camp' wants to mean theatrical, the sense the surface plays on; it is a military base.
explanation.definitionFit: A garrison is a body of troops stationed in a fort, and by extension the military camp itself.

clue.text: State of one who swings both ways when penetrated by mystic symbol

indicators.note: something penetrated has another thing pushed inside it

blocks.note: BI is short for bisexual
a rune is an old letter credited with magic power

explanation.surface: The condition of a bisexual person pierced by an occult sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State of' reads like 'condition of'; 'State' alone is the country, and 'of' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunei is an independent sultanate on Borneo, a sovereign state in its own right.

clue.text: It should ensure a stiff one doesn't go to waste

definitions.text: It should ensure a stiff one doesn't go to waste

blocks.clueFragment: It should ensure a stiff one doesn't go to waste
blocks.note: surface reading: making sure an erection or a strong drink isn't squandered

blocks.clueFragment: It should ensure a stiff one doesn't go to waste
blocks.note: setter's reading: preserving a corpse so that it does not decay

explanation.walkthrough: A stiff is slang for a dead body, and 'waste' hints at wasting away.
explanation.definitionFit: The process preserves a dead body with chemicals to delay decomposition.

clue.text: Obsession, cutting end off cute penis?

indicators.note: cutting an end off removes the last letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: a coy, childish name for the male member

explanation.surface: A fixation on circumcising a sweetly named organ.
explanation.walkthrough: THINGY loses its final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a thing about something is an idiom for being fixated on it, so thing can mean a fixation.

clue.text: ''Milking us rotten,'' his people cried when he'd gone

definitions.text: his people cried when he'd gone

indicators.note: rotten things are spoiled and fall apart, so the quoted letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: The subjects of a tyrant complain he bled them dry, then weep at his funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: North Koreans were filmed weeping en masse when the dictator died in 1994.
explanation.definitionFit: The founding North Korean dictator's death in 1994 was met with staged mass public grief.

clue.text: Expecting to get excited by article on not working

blocks.note: up as in worked up
the definite article
duff is British slang for broken or useless

explanation.surface: Waiting to be aroused by a story about being out of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expecting' looks like anticipation; it means pregnant.
explanation.definitionFit: Up the duff is British slang for pregnant, as is expecting.

clue.text: Pinochet's leader again — to a barmy part of Argentina

indicators.note: the leader is whatever goes first, so only the opening letter of the dictator's name is used
barmy is British slang for crazy, so the letters beside it go haywire

blocks.note: the opening letter of the Chilean dictator's name
taken as written, part of the fodder
taken as written, the rest of the fodder

explanation.surface: Chile's dictator, who sided with Britain in the Falklands War, eyes a mad Argentine region again.
explanation.definitionFit: Patagonia is the southern region of South America, much of it lying in Argentina.

clue.text: A perv iffy about a French johnny-come-lately

indicators.note: iffy means dodgy and about means all around, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken letter by letter
un is French for a

explanation.surface: A dodgy pervert hangs round a Frenchman who arrived late.
explanation.definitionFit: A parvenu is an upstart newcomer to wealth or status, a recent arrival lacking breeding.

clue.text: Good to be close to a bunch of young ones for a pop star has-been?

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
a litter is a brood of young animals

explanation.surface: A disgraced pop idol wants to be near children; a dark Private Eye joke.
explanation.walkthrough: Gary Glitter, a 1970s British glam-rock star, was convicted of child sex offences in Vietnam in 2006.
explanation.definitionFit: Glitter is the stage name of a faded 1970s pop singer, hence a has-been.

clue.text: Bill squeezes wobbly tit — it practically hits the roof

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady, so the word after it is shaken into a new order
to squeeze something is to hold it tightly within, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: AC is short for account, a bill
the word taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A man called Bill grabs at a breast, and the outrage goes through the roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hits the roof' sounds like fury; the definition means the room right under the roof.
explanation.definitionFit: An attic is the space just under a house's roof, so it all but touches it.

clue.text: Hard stuff, being firm and hard inside kinky Lola

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the name's letters are bent into a new order
the firm and the hard pieces go within the other letters

blocks.note: taken as written as the anagram fodder
CO is short for company, a firm
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Something firm and hard inside a kinky woman called Lola; a smutty double entendre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard stuff' reads as smut; it means spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard stuff is an idiom for strong liquor, which is alcohol.

clue.text: All actors in film hugging Loach endlessly, in case

indicators.note: without its end, the director's first name loses its final letter
to hug is to hold within your arms, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: the cast is a film's whole set of actors
Ken Loach is a British film director; his first name loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A whole film cast embraces the director Ken Loach.
explanation.definitionFit: A casket is a small box for jewels or valuables, so it is a kind of case.

clue.text: Awkward Blair finally taken to Bush's heart — jerk!

indicators.note: finally points at the closing letter of the Prime Minister's name
the heart of a word is its middle, so only the central letters of the President's name are kept

blocks.note: the final letter of Tony Blair's surname
the middle two letters of George W Bush's surname
a tic is an involuntary twitch

explanation.surface: Blair, ungainly and awkward, gets close to George Bush, who is insulted as a jerk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk!' reads as an insult hurled at Bush; it is the twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustic means countrified and unsophisticated, hence clumsy or unpolished in manner.

clue.text: Sun pissed by Rush

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for sun
urinated, the literal sense of the vulgar word

explanation.surface: The tabloid's drunk, according to the American shock jock Rush Limbaugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pissed' wants to mean drunk, the British sense; here it is urinated.
explanation.definitionFit: To speed is to go very fast, to hurry or rush.

clue.text: Possibly law-breaking parents' kisses

blocks.note: first meaning: mothers and fathers who smack their children, which British law was then restricting
second meaning: British slang for loud kisses

explanation.surface: Mums and dads whose kisses might somehow fall foul of the law.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes the kisses belong to the parents; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Smacker is slang for a loud kiss, and it also names anyone who hits a child as punishment.

clue.text: Cameron would like to make his party so palatable — not dead!

definitions.text: Cameron would like to make his party so

indicators.note: not here means without, so the letter for the word after it is left out

blocks.note: tasty, delightful to eat
D is the standard abbreviation for dead; this letter goes

explanation.surface: The Tory leader wants voters to find his party appetising, not a corpse.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2006 David Cameron, new Conservative leader, was trying to make the party winnable again.
explanation.definitionFit: Cameron's goal was a party that voters would choose, one capable of winning a general election.

clue.text: (see 5dn.)
Pad produced by American when gobbled by weed

indicators.note: something gobbled is swallowed, so it ends up inside the other piece

blocks.note: to hoe is to weed with a garden blade
US is short for American

explanation.surface: A writing pad made by an American who has been eaten by a weed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weed' is a verb here, not a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Pad is slang for one's home or flat, a place to live.

clue.text: Kissinger's other tit collection?

indicators.note: Henry Kissinger's heavy German accent changes how a word sounds when he says it

blocks.note: the word in Kissinger's German accent, with the th coming out as d

explanation.surface: A joke about the US statesman's second set of breasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tit' here means a teat, and a cow's udder holds several.
explanation.definitionFit: An udder is the bag of a cow's mammary glands with several teats, a group of them.

clue.text: Buy a biog. of Beckham, say? Don't be a total nerd!

definitions.text: Buy a biog. of Beckham, say?

blocks.clueFragment: Buy a biog. of Beckham, say?
blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: obtain a life story of a celebrity
second meaning: the put-down telling someone to stop being so dull

explanation.surface: Mocking someone who buys a footballer's biography as a sad obsessive.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'life' is a biography, so the first half takes the phrase literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom tells someone obsessive or boring to find more interesting things to do.
